title: ProxyPose: 6-DoF Pose Tracking via Video-to-Video Translation
hook: Tracking a moving object's 3D pose normally needs a 3D model, depth, or masks. This method needs none of that — it translates video into a synthetic proxy, then solves the easy version of the problem.
key_points: Standard 6-DoF pose tracking needs extra inputs beyond video — 3D models, depth maps, masks, or learned features — and struggles with textureless, transparent, reflective, or deformable surfaces.

ProxyPose recasts the whole problem as video-to-video translation: given a video and one marked pixel, a fine-tuned video diffusion model generates a proxy video of a synthetic polyhedron undergoing the same local rigid-body motion.
Because the proxy's geometry and appearance are known by construction, recovering its 6-DoF trajectory reduces to classical, off-the-shelf pose estimation.
The hard part of pose tracking — handling difficult materials, occlusions, deformations — gets absorbed into the video-translation step, which leans on large-scale video pretraining.
State-of-the-art accuracy without the extra inputs competing methods need, after fine-tuning only on synthetic data; also extends to face tracking, camera pose, and challenging in-the-wild scenes.
content_html: Tracking exactly how an object moves through 3D space — its full 6-degree-of-freedom pose — usually requires giving the system extra help: a 3D model of the object, a depth sensor, or at least a clean mask. ProxyPose needs none of that, by turning the hard perception problem into a video generation problem instead.
extra_html: Given only a video and a single marked pixel in the first frame, a fine-tuned video diffusion model translates the input into a proxy video — a synthetic clip showing a colored polyhedron undergoing exactly the same local rigid-body motion as the marked surface region. Because the proxy's geometry and appearance are known by construction, recovering its full 6-DoF trajectory reduces to classical pose estimation with off-the-shelf solvers. The trick is where the hard work goes: large-scale video pretraining absorbs the genuinely difficult parts of the problem — textureless surfaces, transparency, reflections, occlusion, deformation — into the translation step, while the actual pose math operates on pixel-level output with no assumptions about object identity or global rigidity. ProxyPose reaches state-of-the-art 6-DoF tracking accuracy without the extra inputs competing methods require, after fine-tuning the video model only on synthetic data, and the authors show the same recipe extends to face tracking, camera pose estimation, and in-the-wild scenes existing approaches can't handle. Ruihang Zhang and colleagues, arXiv 2026.

related.title: ReChannel: Repurposing Text-to-Image Diffusion for Dense Prediction
related.hook: Depth maps and masks get generated as if they were images, decoded through the same interface as RGB pixels. This paper swaps that for a tiny linear head that's 2.5x faster.

related.title: High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion (Stable Diffusion)
related.hook: Running diffusion on raw pixels is brutally expensive. Do it in a compressed latent space instead, and high-res text-to-image becomes cheap enough to run on a consumer GPU.

flashcards.prompt: What's the core reframing ProxyPose uses to solve 6-DoF pose tracking?
flashcards.back_html: It recasts pose tracking as video-to-video translation: a fine-tuned video diffusion model turns the input video into a synthetic proxy video of a colored polyhedron moving the same way, and since the proxy's geometry is known, tracking it reduces to classical pose estimation.

flashcards.prompt: Why does ProxyPose handle textureless, transparent, or deformable surfaces better than methods requiring 3D models or depth maps?

choices.text: The hardest perceptual challenges get absorbed into the video-translation step, which leans on large-scale video pretraining rather than needing explicit geometric inputs
It uses a more powerful depth sensor than competing methods
It only works on rigid, opaque objects and avoids the hard cases entirely
It requires a precise 3D CAD model as an extra input

flashcards.explanation_html: Instead of relying on explicit 3D models, depth, or masks, ProxyPose pushes the hardest parts of perception (occlusion, unusual materials, deformation) into a video diffusion model pretrained at scale, then solves only the easy, well-posed geometry problem on its synthetic proxy output.
